title: Banda's end, 1716
hookLine: captured with hundreds of Sikhs, Banda is executed in Delhi without renouncing his faith

lines: JUST SAY YOU DIDN'T MEAN IT.
cards: Just say you didn't mean it. Just sign here. Just go along, and this all goes away.
An easy way out usually comes with small stakes: a grade, a job, a friendship. Now raise the stakes. The easy way out is your life, and all it costs is saying you no longer believe what you believe.
In the spring of 1716, in Delhi, hundreds of Sikhs were offered exactly that.

teach.b: After Sirhind, the Mughal empire turned its full weight on Banda. For five years he fought and retreated through the hills and plains of Punjab.
In 1715 his forces were surrounded at a walled compound near the village of Gurdas Nangal. The siege lasted about eight months. Food ran out; people ate leaves and bark.
In December, starving, they were captured. Banda and hundreds of Sikhs were marched to Delhi in chains and paraded through the streets. Then, for about a week, a group was executed each day.

teach.h: DELHI — LIFE OFFERED FOR THE FAITH.
teach.b: Each was offered life if they gave up their faith.
Accounts, including a letter written at the time by two English envoys in Delhi, say not one of them accepted. Sikhs tell a story from those days.
A mother pleaded for her young son, saying he wasn't really a Sikh, and won a pardon. The boy refused it. His mother was mistaken, he said; he was a Sikh, and he would stand with the others.
In June 1716, Banda himself was executed, after being forced to watch his small son killed before him. He did not renounce his faith. It's a terrible story, and Sikhs don't tell it for thrills.
They tell it the way a family remembers its hardest year.

It's part of why Ardas, the daily Sikh prayer, remembers those who gave their lives rather than give up their faith. The question it leaves isn't, could I survive that? Almost none of us will face it.
When the easy way out is offered, what am I true to?

how: Sikhs remember Banda Singh Bahadur and the Sikhs executed with him in Delhi in 1716 as shaheeds, martyrs; Ardas, said daily, honors those who gave their lives rather than give up their faith.

o: a peace treaty that closed the Sikh-Mughal war
dying in Delhi rather than give up the faith
a defeat that ended Sikh resistance for good

games.q: the last years — tap the pairs.

s: the captured Sikhs were offered their lives to give up their faith
Banda escaped to the hills and died old
he was executed in Delhi in June 1716.
the boy pardoned at his mother's plea took the pardon
the story Sikhs tell says he refused it and stood with the others.

games.q: you're the boy in Delhi. your mother has won you a pardon by saying you aren't a Sikh. what do you do?
o: say she's mistaken: you're a Sikh, and stand with the others.
run while no one is looking.
games.why: the story Sikhs tell says he refused the pardon. it's remembered as the whole company in a single choice.

practice: Sit quietly for a moment with the people of this story; you don't need to picture anything painful, just let there be a pause, the way a room goes quiet when a family remembers.
Then name one value you want to keep even when it costs a little: honesty, kindness, keeping your word, showing up. Think of one place it might be tested, and decide now to stay true there.

wordCard.voice: Banda's end. Captured after a long siege, Banda and hundreds of Sikhs were executed in Delhi in 1716, and none gave up their faith to live.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: shaheed, a martyr, one who bears witness with their life; a word shared with Persian and Arabic.

carryVoice: Your line: true to the end. Not one of them accepted. Day two hundred eighty-four.
